content: Lycopene is a bright red carotenoid pigment and a phytochemical predominantly found in tomatoes and other red fruits. It is the most abundant carotenoid in the human body and is recognized as one of the most potent carotenoid antioxidants. The name lycopene is derived from the botanical classification of the tomato, Solanum lycopersicum (formerly Lycopersicon esculentum). Structure and Chemistry Lycopene is a terpene molecule composed of eight isoprene units. Its red coloration is attributed to the presence of numerous conjugated carbon double bonds within its structure. These double bonds lower the energy required for electrons to transition to higher energy states, enabling the molecule to absorb visible light at longer wavelengths, which results in its red appearance. When lycopene undergoes oxidation, such as through reactions with bleaches or acids, the carbon double bonds are broken, fragmenting the molecule into smaller compounds that each contain a double bond to an oxygen atom. Although these smaller molecules still possess chromophoric properties due to the C=O bonds, their reduced size prevents them from absorbing sufficient light to appear colorful. Similarly, if lycopene is reduced, the double bonds may be converted into single bonds, which diminishes its ability to absorb light and alters its coloration. Dietary Sources Lycopene is abundant in fruits and vegetables such as tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit, pink guava, papaya, gac, and rosehip. Unlike many other nutrients, such as vitamin C, which degrade during cooking, the bioavailability of lycopene increases with processing. For instance, lycopene in tomato paste is four times more bioavailable than in fresh tomatoes. This is because lycopene is highly insoluble in water and tightly bound to the vegetable's fiber matrix. Processed tomato products, including pasteurized tomato juice, soups, sauces, and ketchup, contain the highest concentrations of bioavailable lycopene. Cooking and crushing tomatoes, as occurs during canning, and serving them in oil-rich dishes, such as spaghetti sauce or pizza, significantly enhance the absorption of lycopene from the digestive tract into the bloodstream. Since lycopene is fat-soluble, the presence of oil facilitates its absorption. Production Lycopene can be extracted from natural sources such as tomatoes and other fruits and vegetables. Additionally, it can be obtained from the fungus Blakeslea trispora, which serves as an alternative source for its production. Nutritional Benefits Lycopene is the most effective carotenoid in neutralizing singlet oxygen, a reactive oxygen species. It is 100 times more efficient in quenching singlet oxygen than vitamin E, which itself is 125 times more effective than glutathione, a water-soluble antioxidant. Due to its potent antioxidant properties, lycopene has been studied for its potential health benefits. Early research suggested that lycopene consumption might have a positive impact on conditions such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, osteoporosis, and male infertility. However, more recent studies have cast doubt on some of these claims, particularly regarding cancer prevention. In fact, beta-carotene, a related antioxidant, has been associated with an increased incidence of prostate cancer in certain studies. Food Coloring Lycopene is widely used as a food coloring agent due to its natural abundance and vibrant red hue. However, it is not water-soluble and readily stains porous materials, including most plastics. While fresh tomato stains can be removed from fabrics relatively easily, lycopene diffuses into plastics, making the stains nearly impossible to remove using hot water, soap, or detergent. Bleach, however, can degrade lycopene and eliminate the stain. Plastics are particularly prone to staining when they are heated, scratched, oiled, or exposed to acidic conditions. Formulations Available Lycopene is commercially available in combination with other carotenoids and antioxidants. It is marketed under various brand names by pharmaceutical companies. Some commonly available formulations include LYCORED, LYNET, and LYCORICH.
